https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An excerpt from the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) 2021 Elections booklet, presenting candidate election statements for the Region 8 seat on the MASB Board of Directors (a three-year term). The document notes there were 22 candidates for the MASB Board of Directors overall; the included pages cover three Region 8 (Oakland County) candidates. It was provided to the Troy Board of Education for the February 23, 2021 meeting so the Board could cast its member-district vote.

Candidate 1 - Sandra Dukhie, Ferndale Public Schools, Oakland County. Time served: four years; offices held: Vice President. Her statement frames education as "the great equalizer" and emphasizes equity and inclusion. She co-authored her district's resolution declaring racism a public health crisis, is an active member of the Oakland County Council for Diversity Equity and Inclusion, and hosted/facilitated a 30-Day Racial Equity Habit Building Challenge on social media (adapted from Eddie Moore Jr.'s 21-day challenge). She has worked in public education since 1999, is the parent of five sons, was appointed to the Ferndale School Board in March 2017 and elected in November 2018, and chairs the Ferndale Inclusion Network.

Candidate 2 - Mary Hanser, Oxford Community Schools, Oakland County. Time served: two years. MASB certifications: Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit. She seeks to advocate for and support Region 8 districts and to make Michigan a "public school destination" through equitable funding and well-trained boards. She serves on the Oakland County School Board Association (OCSBA) Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Committee and the OCSBA Government Relations Committee, earned her CBA Certification and Award of Merit within her first two years, and completed coursework for the Advocacy Skills Specialty. Prior community service includes high school robotics team mentor, FIRST Robotics Competition volunteer, and the Macomb County Commission on Women. She holds a Bachelor of Business Administration from Walsh College and has worked in the nonprofit, corporate, and small-business sectors.

Candidate 3 - Birgit McQuiston, Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County. Time served: nine years; offices held: Vice President and Secretary. MASB certifications: Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, and Master Diamond Award (earned 2019). First elected to the Lake Orion Board in May 2011; elected to her third term in November 2020. Her committee work includes policy, curriculum, board self-assessment, superintendent evaluation, Lamp of Learning, and Government Relations; she has served as president, vice president, and secretary, and traveled to Lansing to address the Senate and House education committees advocating for local control and against unfunded mandates. She is in her third year on the OCSBA Board of Directors (secretary two years) and was appointed to the MASB Resolutions & Bylaws Committee in 2018. Her statement (truncated) describes running for the MASB Board of Directors to continue developing board leadership across Oakland County's 201 trustees.

The document is informational campaign material to guide the Troy Board's Region 8 vote and contains no Troy-specific action or figures.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A January 26, 2021 legal memorandum from Collins & Blaha, P.C. (attorneys Gary J. Collins and John C. Kava) to the International Academy Governing Body, care of Troy Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky, analyzing amendments to the International Academy Consortium Agreement proposed by Bloomfield Hills Schools on November 24, 2020. Bloomfield had not approved the 2020 Consortium Agreement but continued participating; its new proposal drops earlier governance objections and focuses on clean-up and clarification. Counsel recommends the six substantive amendments as agreeable and attaches a redlined amendment (Exhibit A) and a draft approval resolution (Exhibit B).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A legal memorandum reviewing Bloomfield Hills Schools' proposed amendments to the International Academy (IA) Consortium Agreement, prepared for the IA Governing Body.

Parties / routing
- From: Gary J. Collins, Esq. and John C. Kava, Esq., Collins & Blaha, P.C.
- To: International Academy Governing Body, c/o Dr. Richard M. Machesky, Superintendent, Troy School District
- Date: January 26, 2021
- Re: Requested Consortium Agreement Amendments (proposal originally sent by Bloomfield Nov. 24, 2020)

Background
Bloomfield's Board did not approve the Consortium Agreement the other IA districts approved in summer 2020, but has continued to participate. It previously raised governance-structure and principal-employment concerns; the new proposal drops most of those and focuses on clean-up/clarification.

Six substantive proposed amendments
1. Clarify the definition of "Academy" to note the Consortium operates at more than one campus.
2. Article III, Sec. 3(A): new participant admission also requires affirmative vote of the Fiscal Agent Superintendent for the relevant campus, and must specify Shares allotted.
3. Article IV, Sec. 1(B)(1): more detailed list of overhead costs allocable per campus (IB license fees, legal fees, Principal/shared-administrator salaries, benefits, insurance).
4. Article IV, Sec. 1(C): remove reference to Superintendent's "designee" - Superintendents must act personally.
5. Article IV, Sec. 1(G)(3): suspensions longer than ten days must be referred to the student's district of residence for due process.
6. Appendices (participant list; Appendix B billing/payments) must be updated.

Attachments / purpose
Exhibit A - redlined First Amendment; Exhibit B - draft resolution for each district's board. Counsel finds the amendments agreeable and suitable for distribution to participating districts for approval.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum from the law firm Collins & Blaha, P.C., dated January 26, 2021, addressed to the International Academy (IA) Governing Body in care of Dr. Richard M. Machesky, Superintendent of the Troy School District (the IA's fiscal agent). The memo is signed by attorneys Gary J. Collins, Esq. and John C. Kava, Esq., and its subject is requested Consortium Agreement amendments. It was included in the February 23, 2021 Troy Board of Education meeting packet.

Background: Bloomfield Hills Schools ("Bloomfield") sent a proposed International Academy Consortium Agreement Amendment to the Governing Body on November 24, 2020. The firm reviewed the proposal and discussed it with Bloomfield's legal counsel; Governing Body members also spoke with the participating districts' superintendents. Bloomfield's Board of Education had not approved the Consortium Agreement that the other IA districts approved in summer 2020, though Bloomfield has continued to participate in the Consortium. Bloomfield had previously raised concerns about the 2020 Agreement's governance structure and other provisions, including employment of the principal. The latest proposed amendment omits many of those prior issues and instead focuses on clean-up and clarification; counsel believes the amendments are agreeable to the IA Consortium members and would let the Consortium move forward with all currently participating districts.

The six substantive proposed amendments (detailed in redlined Exhibit A) are:
1. Clarify in the definition of "Academy" that the Consortium operates at more than one campus.
2. Amend Article III, Section 3(A) (admission of new participants) so that, in addition to Governing Body approval, the Superintendent of the Fiscal Agent for the campus where the new participant will be located must vote in the affirmative for the action to be effective; the approval must also specify the number of Shares allotted to the new district.
3. Amend Article IV, Section 1(B)(1) (Governing Body powers) to include a more detailed list of overhead costs allocable to each campus, including IB license fees, legal fees and expenses, and costs to employ the Principal and other administrators shared by all three campuses (salaries, benefits, and insurance premiums).
4. Amend Article IV, Section 1(C) to remove the reference to the Superintendent's "designee," so that Superintendents themselves must act rather than designees who do not regularly attend meetings.
5. Amend Article IV, Section 1(G)(3) to state that disciplinary action resulting in a suspension of longer than ten days must be referred to the student's district of residence, which shall provide due process to the student.
6. Require that the Appendices to the Agreement be updated, including the list of Consortium participants and Appendix B governing how payments and billing operate; counsel suggests the business managers review Appendix B.

Attachments: Exhibit A is a redlined version of Bloomfield's proposed "First Amendment to Amended and Restated International Academy Consortium Agreement"; Exhibit B is a draft resolution that each participating school district may use to have its own board approve the amendment. The memo's recitals note the Amended and Restated Agreement was ratified by a specified number of school districts (blank in the draft) and that additional districts desire to ratify it. Counsel recommends the Governing Body review the amendment and then distribute the memo and attachments to the Consortium's participating districts for review and approval, and invites questions. Document reference: 4819-1377-8905, v.1.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation titled "Troy School District Pupil Enrollment Projection Study Update, November 2020," prepared by Plante Moran Cresa (PMC) and delivered to the Board of Education (packet dated for board update 12-01-2020; presented at the February 23, 2021 meeting).

Firm overview: PMC describes itself as offering collective expertise (planners, architects, engineers, construction experts, financial advisors, real estate professionals) and full-service K-12 support from concept to completion, including enrollment projections recognized by the Michigan Department of Treasury, bond planning/feasibility studies, program management, and real estate asset positioning, with independent, conflict-free advice.

Methodology: PMC's process uses demographic growth analysis, GIS, US Census Bureau data, Core Base Statistical Area analysis, comparisons at the primary (district), county, and state levels, and the Cohort Survival method (DS 4061).

Troy School District demographics (2020): Median age of householder 55.1; total number of families 18,603; households with school-age children 11,233 (43.9% of households with children); enrolled school-aged children 12,430. Enrollment splits: Public PK 43.47% / Private PK 56.53%; Public K-12 89.54% / Private K-12 10.46%.

District-wide projected pupil enrollment figures shown: Birth Year 2015 with 13,547 births; K% of Births 5.97%; K-12 Enrollment 12,764; number difference -113; percent growth -0.87%; total 12,962.

Key takeaways comparing 2018 to 2020 (PEPS overview):
- Median age of householder: 54.0 to 55.1 (+1.1 years)
- Total housing units: 26,906 to 27,150 (+244 units)
- Total families: 18,583 to 18,603 (+20 families)
- Households with school age: 11,603 to 11,233 (-370 households)
- Enrolled school-aged children: 13,017 to 12,430 (-587 children)
- Enrolled in Public PK: 43.25% to 43.47% (+0.22%)
- Enrolled in Private PK: 56.75% to 56.53% (-0.22%)
- Enrolled in Public K-12: 89.96% to 89.54% (-0.42%)
- Enrolled in Private K-12: 10.04% to 10.46% (+0.42%)
- K% county birth enrolled: 6.31% to 5.97% (-0.34%)
- PMC 2020 Projection versus Actual K-12: 12,760 projected versus 12,764 actual (+4 pupils)

The presentation emphasizes the accuracy of PMC's prior forecast (a +4 pupil variance between the 2020 projection and actual enrollment) and portrays a maturing, aging community with modest housing growth but declining numbers of school-aged children and households with school-age children, supporting a slight projected enrollment decline. The study is intended as an independent, demographically grounded tool to inform the district's facilities, bond, and long-range budget planning. The deck concludes with a Questions/Answers section.

This document is the agenda cover sheet for item 10.B. of the Troy Board of Education Regular Meeting held March 16, 2021, filed under the "Other" section, presenting a Consideration titled "Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan."

The background explains that Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of Pre-K through Post High School education. Under this order, school districts in Michigan must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the various phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan. Each district must submit a reconfirmation plan to its Board of Education for approval on a monthly basis, and once approved, each district must post its Preparedness Plan on the district's website home page for public access. At this meeting, the Board is being asked to approve the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan.

The recommended action is to adopt the suggested resolution, which reads: "Be it therefore resolved that the Troy Board of Education approves the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan." The document includes blank "Moved by" and "Supported by" lines and a roll call vote template listing the seven board members: Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, and Hammond, with blank Yes and No tally lines.

This is a routine, recurring monthly compliance item mandated by state pandemic executive orders. The cover sheet itself does not contain the text of the Preparedness & Response Plan, specific health protocols, phase determinations, or the outcome of the vote; it establishes only the procedural request and the legal basis for the monthly reconfirmation requirement.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A February 28, 2021 memorandum from Assistant Superintendent of Business Services Rick West to Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky recommends that the Troy School District Board of Education authorize refinancing of the district's 2014 bonds and possibly its 2012 bonds. Analysis by PFM Financial Advisors projects the refinancing would save the community approximately $2.1 million over the life of the bond payments while maintaining the current 4.1-mill debt levy for two years, preserving the option of a no-increase bond campaign in 2022.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Memorandum dated February 28, 2021 from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, to Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky, recommending a bond refinancing strategy for consideration at the March 16, 2021 Board meeting.

Recommendation
- Authorize refinancing of the district's 2014 bonds and possibly its 2012 bonds.
- Projected savings of approximately $2.1 million over the duration of the bond payments.
- Structure the refinance to maintain the current levy of 4.1 mills to meet the annual debt obligation for the next two years.

Strategic purpose
- Maintaining the current 4.1-mill levy preserves the option to offer the community a no-increase bond campaign in 2022 should the Board desire.
- Without refinancing, the district would forgo the $2.1 million savings and might need to reduce the levy by as much as 0.5 mills for the 2021-2022 taxable year, which would jeopardize the ability to advertise a no-increase bond campaign.

Supporting materials
- Parameters and financial analysis prepared by PFM Financial Advisors are attached (Bondspecs Ref 2014_2012 Troy 2021 UTGO.pdf).
- The document will be used by the district's attorney to draft the authorizing resolution recommended for the March 16 meeting.

Who/where
Troy School District Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; phone 248.823.4022.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Memorandum on Troy School District Business Office letterhead (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; phone 248.823.4022; fax 248.823.4013), dated February 28, 2021, addressed to Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services. The subject is "Bond Refinancing Strategy."

West recommends that the Board of Education consider authorizing the refinancing of the district's 2014 bonds and possibly its 2012 bonds. Current analysis projects that the refinancing will save the community approximately $2.1 million over the duration of the bond payments. The memo states that the refinance would be structured to maintain the district's current levy of 4.1 mills to meet the annual debt obligation for the next two years.

A central strategic rationale is that maintaining the current 4.1-mill levy would allow the district to provide an option to the community for a no-increase bond campaign in 2022, should the Board desire to pursue one. West warns that absent the refinancing and restructuring of the current debt, the district would forgo the $2.1 million in savings and would need to consider reducing the current levy by as much as 0.5 mills for the 2021-2022 taxable year. Any such reduction in the levy would jeopardize the district's ability to advertise a no-increase bond campaign.

The memo notes that the parameters and financial analysis supporting the refinancing were prepared by PFM Financial Advisors and are attached (the attachment is titled "Bondspecs Ref 2014_2012 Troy 2021 UTGO.pdf"). That document was to be used by the district's attorney to draft the necessary authorizing resolution, which West indicates would be recommended for the Board's consideration at their meeting on Tuesday, March 16, 2021. This memo is the business-office recommendation underlying agenda item 8.A at the March 16, 2021 Regular Meeting of the Board of Education.

What it is
A resolution of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, authorizing the issuance of "2021 Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation) (Taxable)," set within the minutes of the regular meeting conducted electronically on March 16, 2021 at 7:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

Legal basis
- Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended (the Revised Municipal Finance Act), permitting refunding of funded indebtedness.
- Requires the district to be qualified or obtain prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

Bonds being refunded (Prior Bonds)
- 2012 Refunding Bonds (General Obligation - Unlimited Tax), dated December 20, 2012.
- 2014 School Building and Site Bonds (General Obligation - Unlimited Tax), dated January 29, 2014.

Key authorized terms

- Purpose: advance refund all or a portion of the callable maturities of the Prior Bonds on a taxable basis and pay costs of issuance.
- Denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples; mature May 1; interest payable semiannually May 1 and November 1.
- Interest rate not exceeding 4.00% per annum.
- Net present value savings must be not less than 1.00% of projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds.
- Sale price not less than 99% and no more than 105% of principal.

- May be issued as serial or term bonds, in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company, New York.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Formal resolution captioned "TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, COUNTY OF OAKLAND, STATE OF MICHIGAN, RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING 2021 REFUNDING BONDS (UNLIMITED TAX GENERAL OBLIGATION) (TAXABLE)." It is framed as the minutes of a regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District conducted electronically on March 16, 2021, at 7:00 p.m. prevailing Eastern Time, with blanks for present/absent members and for the member offering and the member supporting the resolution.

Recitals (WHEREAS clauses): Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, the Revised Municipal Finance Act (the "Act"), permits the district to refund all or part of its funded indebtedness. The district previously issued its 2012 Refunding Bonds (General Obligation - Unlimited Tax), dated December 20, 2012 (the "2012 Bonds"), and its 2014 School Building and Site Bonds (General Obligation - Unlimited Tax), dated January 29, 2014 (the "2014 Bonds"), together the "Prior Bonds." The district's Municipal Advisor advised that a net present value savings of debt service costs may be achieved by issuing refunding bonds. The district determined it is in its best interest to issue bonds not to exceed Forty-Five Million Dollars ($45,000,000) to advance refund all or a portion of the callable maturities of the Prior Bonds (the "Refunded Bonds") on a taxable basis. The district must either be qualified or obtain prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury ("Treasury").

Resolved provisions: (1) Authorization of Bonds - bonds designated "2021 Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation) (Taxable)" are authorized to be issued in one or more series, in aggregate principal amount not to exceed $45,000,000, or such lesser amount as determined by the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually (each an "Authorized Officer"), for the purpose of refunding the Refunded Bonds and paying costs of issuance. (2) Bond Details - bonds registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of delivery or another date determined by the Authorized Officer, numbered as determined by the Transfer Agent. Bonds mature on May 1 in years and amounts determined at sale, and bear interest at rates determined upon sale not exceeding four percent (4.00%) per annum, payable semiannually on May 1 and November 1. The net present value savings to be realized must be not less than one percent (1.00%) of the projected debt service payable on the Refunded Bonds absent the refunding, based on Treasury guidelines. The bonds are to be sold at a price not less than 99% and no more than 105% of principal amount.

Additional terms: The bonds may be issued as serial or term bonds or both and are subject to optional redemption prior to maturity at times and prices determined by the Authorized Officer; term bonds designated by the original purchaser are subject to mandatory redemption per the maturity schedule in the Notice of Sale. Principal is payable at a bank or trust company selected by an Authorized Officer, serving as registrar and Transfer Agent, upon presentation and surrender of the bond. Interest is paid by check drawn on the Transfer Agent, mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to the payment date. The bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, and official notice of redemption is given by the Transfer Agent on behalf of the district unless waived by a registered owner.

The document is primarily graphical (slides of design boards), so the extracted text consists mainly of slide labels and captions rather than narrative content. It accompanies agenda item 8.B at the March 16, 2021 Regular Meeting of the Board of Education, which concerns Bid Package 32 renovation work.

The presentation is organized around a series of "Architectural Finishes" boards and a "Composite Furniture Plan." It depicts the intended interior design and functional zoning of the renovated media center. Named zones and concept elements include: a Cafe; a "Genius Bar" (shown as a concept image); a "Floor Pattern" study; a "Campfire" gathering area; "Small Groups" areas labeled A, B, C, and D under a "Together & Alone" concept; "Circulation"; and a "Large Group Instruction & Presentation" area. "Furniture Finishes" boards are also included.

For the "Book Stacks," the presentation specifies perimeter wall shelving that is 90 inches high with 6 shelves, along with double-sided mobile shelving. The presentation closes with a "Thank You!" slide. Overall, the document conveys the design intent, finishes palette, furniture layout, and the range of flexible learning and gathering spaces planned for the Troy High School Media Center renovation, providing the Board with a visual reference for the construction work being awarded under Bid Package 32.

What it is
Operations Department memorandum (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083) dated February 25, 2021, from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent - Business Services, regarding RFP 9921 - 2021 Site Work Paving Program #2.

Scope of work
- Site construction work at the Transportation and Costello Elementary sites.
- Enlarging and restoration of the stormwater retention basin plus drain modifications at the Transportation Building.
- Slurry sealcoating of the Transportation parking lot and an isolated area of the Costello Elementary parking lot.

Bids and recommended awards
- RFP resulted in 3 bids (bid summary attached).
- Package #1 - Costello Elementary: Best Asphalt, Inc. - $24,590.00
- Package #2 - Transportation Building (including Alternate #1): Asphalt Specialists Inc. (ASI) - $339,000.00
- Contingency (8%): $29,087.20
- TOTAL VALUE: $392,677.20

Review and funding
- Proposals reviewed and post-bid interviews performed by PEA Engineering, Lecole Planners, and Rob Carson.
- A separate Purchase Order per bid project package.
- Funding from the Capital Projects Fund and Building Site & Sinking Fund.
- Cc: Donna Havrilla.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Memorandum on Troy School District Operations Department letterhead (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083; phone 248.823.4050; fax 248.823.4077), dated February 25, 2021, from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent - Business Services. Subject: RFP 9921 - 2021 Site Work Paving Program #2.

RFP #9921 was issued to obtain competitive bids for site construction work at the Transportation and Costello Elementary sites. The scope of work includes enlarging and restoration of the stormwater retention basin along with some drain modifications at the Transportation Building. The scope also includes slurry sealcoating of the Transportation parking lot and an isolated area of the parking lot at Costello Elementary.

The RFP resulted in 3 bids, with a bid summary attached. Carson recommends the following vendors based on low bid for each project package: Package #1 - Costello Elementary - Best Asphalt, Inc. - $24,590.00; Package #2 - Transportation Building (including Alternate #1) - Asphalt Specialists Inc. (ASI) - $339,000.00. A Contingency of 8% adds $29,087.20, for a TOTAL VALUE of $392,677.20.

All proposals were reviewed, and post-bid interviews were performed by PEA Engineering, Lecole Planners, and Carson himself. The memo restates that the total amount of site work to be completed for this recommendation is $392,677.20 including the requested 8% contingency. A separate Purchase Order will be issued for each bid project package. Funding for these purchases will be drawn from the Capital Projects Fund and the Building Site & Sinking Fund. The memo copies Donna Havrilla and lists an attached Bid Summary Tabulation. This memo is the operations recommendation underlying agenda item 8.C at the March 16, 2021 Regular Meeting of the Board of Education.

The document recounts that a 2011 shift from a 3-tier to a 5-tier bussing schedule (to save about $800,000 annually) forced high schools to start at 7:20 a.m., and cites research on adolescent sleep needs and recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Agenda item 10.A. (dated 04.20.21) — a consideration and suggested resolution for the Troy Board of Education to implement "Healthy High School Start Times."

Background
- The Board has studied high school start times for the past four years.
- In 2011, amid the lowest point of state funding, the District shifted from a 3-tier to a 5-tier bussing schedule to cut transportation costs by about $800,000 per year, which staggered elementary/middle start times and required high schools to start at 7:20 a.m.
- Growing evidence indicates earlier high school start times may harm students' social/emotional health and academic achievement.

Proposed decision
Begin implementation of a high school start time of 8:00 a.m. or later for all Troy high schools starting in the 2022-2023 school year.

Resolution rationale (WHEREAS clauses)
- Ties to the five-year District Strategic Plan commencing August 2021 and its commitment to social, emotional, and physical well-being.
- Cites that teenagers require more sleep; sleep deprivation increases risk of depression, anxiety, illness, obesity, athletic injuries, and suicide.
- Notes the American Academy of Pediatrics and at least a dozen national organizations recommend later start times.
- Acknowledges likely impacts on middle/elementary start times, transportation routing, and budget.

Resolved
Directs the Superintendent to immediately begin a Healthy High School Start Time Implementation Plan commencing at the start of the 2022-2023 school year. Includes Yes/No vote lines.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is agenda item 10.A. (Other), dated 04.20.21, a consideration item and suggested resolution presented to the Troy Board of Education titled "Healthy High School Start Times." The recommended action is to adopt the accompanying resolution.

Background narrative: The document states the Troy Board of Education has been studying high school start times for the past four years. It explains that when state funding was cut to its lowest point in 2011, the District decided to shift from a 3-tier bussing schedule to a 5-tier schedule to reduce transportation costs by approximately $800,000 each year. That change staggered start times for elementary and middle schools and required high schools to start at 7:20 a.m. Over the past five years, increasing evidence has shown that earlier high school start times may not be optimal for the social/emotional health or academic achievement of high school students. The Board has determined it is in the best interest of all students to begin implementing a high school start time of 8:00 a.m. or later for all Troy high schools, beginning with the 2022-2023 school year.

Resolution ("Resolution to Implement Healthy High School Start Times"): The suggested resolution includes blank lines for "Moved by" and "Supported by" and a series of WHEREAS clauses establishing rationale: the Board is initiating a five-year District Strategic Plan commencing August 2021; that plan will include the District's continual commitment to the social, emotional, and physical well-being of all; well over three years ago the Board initiated efforts to inform itself about the physiological and developmental sleep needs of teenagers; science has demonstrated teenagers require more sleep than other age groups; sleep deprivation increases the risk of depression, anxiety, illness, obesity, athletic injuries, and suicide; the American Academy of Pediatrics and at least one dozen other national organizations recommend later high school start times; robust scientific research demonstrates later start times lead to more sleep; the Board has welcomed community input and performed due diligence and deliberation; such due diligence led the Board to believe moving to a later start will improve student mental health, safety, attendance, graduation, family happiness, and positive school culture; the Board has determined it is in the best interest of all students to begin implementation of a later high school start for all Troy School District high schools, targeting an optimum start time of 8:00 a.m. or later; and it is understood the implementation will likely impact middle school and elementary school start times, transportation routing and operations, and budget.

The operative clause states: NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Superintendent be directed to immediately begin a Healthy High School Start Time Implementation Plan which will commence at the start of the 2022-2023 school year. The document ends with "Yes" and "No" vote lines. No specific vote tally, mover, or supporter is recorded in the text.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Vendor recommendation letter dated March 24, 2021, from John C. Foster, RCDD, President (of Convergent Technology Partners, the district's procurement advisor), addressed to Beth Soggs, Technology Director, Troy School District, concerning Virtual Infrastructure and Storage Area Network RFP #9914.

Scope: The RFP solicited bids for new servers, storage devices, and a backup solution covering all administrative and instructional data. It also included mandatory alternates to create redundant copies of district data and provide a secure, air-gapped repository.

Procurement timeline: Troy School District issued the RFP on December 18, 2020, posting it to the district website and the State's Sigma site. On January 27, 2021, sealed bids were accepted and opened virtually by Convergent Technology Partners on the district's behalf. Two proposals were received.

Mandatory alternates: (1) an air gap solution securing data backups against ransomware attacks; (2) a second backup appliance located at a secondary site; (3) a data cabinet as specified.

Bid figures. Base bids: Presidio $468,567.12; Logicalis $391,857.06. Alternate pricing included Presidio Mandatory Alternate 1 $286,779.36, Mandatory Alternate 2 $118,835.83, and Mandatory Alternate 3 $4,443.42; Logicalis Mandatory Alternate 1 $90,546.57, Mandatory Alternate 2 $39,164.47, Mandatory Alternate 3 $1,545.69, and a Voluntary Alternate 1 of -$25,015.50.

Evaluation and rationale: Proposals were evaluated for compliance, pricing, technical solution, and acceptance of RFP terms. Discrepancies were found, especially in cyber security: while Logicalis's response provided a minimal level of protection, it did not meet the required air gap solution, and Logicalis omitted required cables that would add approximately $10,000 to its base bid. Presidio, with the Dell/EMC team, has provided and supported the district's existing data center and Cisco networking equipment for over 15 years and has in-depth knowledge of district operations and future needs. Presidio's recommended backup solution is the upgraded version of software in district use for over 12 years, keeping a single vendor for escalations. The solution includes Mandatory Alternate 2 (redundant backup appliance) and, per post-bid conversations, an optional cloud copy providing an immutable, locked-down backup at an additional cost of approximately $34,300.

Recommendation and totals: Award to Presidio. - Apple Authorized Resellers in the U.S. are prohibited from selling Apple Products to private or public educational institutions.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Apple Sole Source Letter (marked 'APPLE CONFIDENTIAL'), dated March 17, 2021, with form reference SCC_US_18February2015, addressed to Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, Troy Public Schools, 4400 Livernois Rd, Troy, MI 48098, and signed by Vanessa Boenig of Apple Inc., U.S. Bids and Sales Contracts Management.

Purpose: The letter informs the district that Apple Inc. is the sole source provider of Apple Products and certain Exclusive products to the organization, thereby supporting a direct purchase in lieu of a competitive RFP.

Definitions provided: 'Apple Products' refers to Services, CTO Products, hardware products, and software products manufactured, distributed, or licensed under the Apple brand name that a customer has paid to acquire or properly licensed from Apple for its own use, excluding any third-party software and all other third-party products. 'Services' means the standard, price-listed services, support, and/or training products sold under the Apple brand name. 'Configure-To-Order Products' or 'CTO Products' are Products Apple modifies from its standard configurations, available only by special order. 'Exclusive' products are products that complement Apple-branded products which only Apple is licensed to resell.

Reseller restrictions: Pursuant to their agreements with Apple, Apple Authorized Resellers in the United States are prohibited from selling Apple Products to private or public educational institutions. Certain Apple authorized cellular phone carriers/providers, including AT&T, Verizon, and Sprint, are authorized to sell the iPhone or iPad to educational institutions. Aside from these exceptions, Apple states it has no present intention to use agents and has not authorized any Apple Authorized Reseller, other than authorized Carriers, to sell Apple Products to the organization. Apple will continue to have a direct sales and purchasing relationship with the district and remain its sole source for all Apple Products.

Section 624 of the Revised School Code, as amended, requires the Troy Board to review the proposed Oakland ISD budget and express support or disapproval.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: Consent agenda item 5.F., dated 05.18.21, of the Troy Board of Education Regular Meeting for May 18, 2021, is a CONSIDERATION titled "Approve Oakland Intermediate School District 2021-2022 Budget." In accordance with Section 624 of the Revised School Code, as amended, the Troy Board of Education is required to review the proposed Oakland Intermediate School District budget and express either its support or disapproval. The Recommended Action is to adopt the resolution. The resolution's WHEREAS clauses restate the statutory framework: (1) Section 624 requires the intermediate school board to submit its proposed General Fund budget no later than May 1 of each year to the board of each constituent district for review; and (2) not later than June 1 of each year, the board of each constituent district shall review the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget, adopt a board resolution expressing its support for or disapproval of the proposed budget, and submit to the intermediate school board any specific objections and proposed changes it has. The operative NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED clauses provide: (1) the board of education has received and reviewed the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget in accordance with Section 624 and, by adoption of this resolution, expresses its support for the proposed budget; (2) the secretary of the board of education or his/her designee shall forward a copy of this resolution to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1; and (3) all resolutions insofar as they conflict with this resolution are rescinded. The document includes "Yes"/"No" vote lines and the notation "Resolution declared adopted," followed by a signature line for the Secretary, Troy Board of Education. A certification block states that the undersigned Secretary certifies the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted by the Troy Board of Education at a regular meeting held on May 18, 2021, the original of which is part of the Board's minutes, and further certifies that notice of the meeting was given to the public under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended. Consent agenda item 5.G. from the Troy School District Board of Education Regular Meeting of May 18, 2021 — a CONSIDERATION adopting a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2021-2022 school year budget.

Key details
- Public hearing date/time: June 15, 2021 at 7:00 p.m., at a special Board meeting.
- Location: Athens High School, 4333 John R, Troy, MI 48085.
- Budget copies available for public inspection at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, 8:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m., Wednesday, June 2, 2021 through Tuesday, June 15, 2021.

Legal requirements cited
- Michigan law requires every local unit of government, including a school district, to hold a public hearing on its proposed budget, with notice at least six days before the hearing.
- The notice must state the time and place and where the proposed budget is available for inspection.
- The notice must include, in 11-point bold face type: "THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING."

Administration
The Board Secretary is authorized to publish notice (substantially in the form of Exhibit A) in a newspaper of general circulation at least six days before the hearing. Exhibit A is signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This internal memorandum, dated April 28, 2021, is from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology for Troy School District (Technology Services, 4420 Livernois, phone 248.823.5060), addressed to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services. Its subject is Elementary Classroom Technology.

The memo transmits an attached recommendation letter from Convergent Technology Partners recommending the award of the Elementary Classroom Technology RFP, designated Bid Number 9925. The RFP and recommendation cover a defined scope of work for elementary classrooms. That scope includes: removal and disposal of the existing Smartboard/projector in each classroom; removal and disposal of the existing classroom audio equipment (speakers, amplifier, and microphone); and the purchase and installation of a new 86-inch TV, a TV wall mount, four ceiling-mounted speakers, an amplifier, and a microphone. The scope also includes all necessary HDMI and power cables.

The base bid response covers all of the listed equipment for the classrooms. In addition, a 10% contingency has been added to the project. According to the memo, that contingency is intended to cover additional materials that may be needed to reinforce walls, to add smaller TVs in other small instructional spaces, and to add technology to new classrooms that may or may not be added in the fall of 2021.

The memorandum functions as the administrative justification supporting the companion resolution before the Board (agenda item 8.A) to award the elementary classroom displays and sound systems bid. It establishes that a competitive RFP process was used, that Convergent Technology Partners served as the district's technical evaluator, and that the recommendation reflects a defined removal-and-replacement standard for classroom audiovisual technology across the elementary buildings. The document does not, in this text, state the dollar amount of the award or the winning vendor; those figures appear in the accompanying resolution.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is an official Apple Inc. Sole Source Letter, marked APPLE CONFIDENTIAL and dated March 17, 2021. It is addressed to Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, Troy Public Schools, 4400 Livernois Rd, Troy, MI 48098, and is signed by Vanessa Boenig of Apple Inc., U.S. Bids and Sales Contracts Management. The letter carries the internal reference code SCC_US_18February2015.

The stated purpose of the letter is to inform the district that Apple Inc. is the sole source provider of Apple Products and certain Exclusive products to the organization. The letter provides formal definitions of the relevant product categories. Apple Products refers to Services, CTO Products, hardware products, and software products manufactured, distributed, or licensed under the Apple brand name that a customer has paid to acquire or properly licensed from Apple for its own use, excluding third-party software and other third-party products. Services means the standard, price-listed services, support, and training products sold under the Apple brand. Configure-To-Order Products, or CTO Products, are products Apple modifies from standard configurations and that are available only by special order. Exclusive products refer to products that complement Apple-branded products that only Apple has a license to resell.

The letter explains the procurement rationale: pursuant to their agreements with Apple, Apple Authorized Resellers in the United States are prohibited from selling Apple Products to private or public educational institutions like the district. It notes an exception that certain Apple-authorized cellular carriers/providers, including AT&T, Verizon, and Sprint, are authorized to sell the iPhone or iPad to educational institutions. Aside from those exceptions, Apple states it has no present intention to use agents and has not authorized any Apple Authorized Reseller, other than authorized carriers, to sell Apple Products to the organization. Apple affirms it will continue to have a direct sales and purchasing relationship with the district and will continue to be the sole source for all Apple Products.

Within the Board meeting, this letter serves as the supporting justification for a sole-source, no-RFP procurement of Apple hardware. It is filed under Business agenda item 8.B alongside a memorandum and resolution to purchase Apple TVs for elementary classrooms, establishing the legal and procurement basis for buying directly from Apple rather than through a competitive bid process.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This internal memorandum is dated April 28, 2021 and is from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology (Troy School District Technology Services, 4420 Livernois, phone 248.823.5060), to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services. The subject is the Elementary Apple TV Purchase.

The memo situates the request within a vision discussed at the April 2021 Board Workshop and Board Meeting: providing elementary classrooms with mobility and flexibility for teaching. The plan is to install an 86-inch TV in each elementary classroom, and a connected Apple TV would allow the classroom teacher to wirelessly display content from an iPad or MacBook directly to the TV from anywhere in the classroom. The Apple TVs therefore complement the larger classroom display standardization described under agenda item 8.A.

On procurement method, the memo explains that an RFP was not issued for this purchase because Apple does sell its products to education through resellers, and a Sole Source letter from Apple is attached to support the direct purchase. Apple has quoted the 4K 32GB Apple TV at $179 per unit.

The recommendation is to purchase 315 Apple TVs at a cost of $179 each, for a total purchase cost of $56,385. The memo states this purchase will be funded from series 3 of the bond.

The document is the administrative justification behind agenda item 8.B and its companion resolution to purchase Elementary Classroom Apple TVs. It documents the educational rationale (wireless casting from iPad/MacBook to the new 86-inch displays), the sole-source procurement basis (Apple's reseller model plus the attached Sole Source letter), the unit price ($179 for the 4K 32GB model), the quantity (315 units), the total cost ($56,385), and the funding source (bond series 3). Note that the companion resolution identifies the funding as the 2019 Capital Projects Fund, while this memo describes the source as series 3 of the bond.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is a formal bid evaluation and award recommendation letter dated April 22, 2021, on the letterhead of Convergent Technology Partners, 6197 Miller Road, Ste #4, Swartz Creek, MI 48473 (phone 810.720.3820; e-mail info@ctpartners.net; website www.ctpartners.net). It is addressed to Beth Soggs, Technology Director, Troy School District, and concerns the Troy High School Media Center AV RFP #9926.

The letter describes the procurement process. On March 29, 2021, Troy School District issued a Request for Proposal soliciting bids for the THS Media Center AV project, and the RFP was posted to the District's website. Convergent also spoke with several vendors about the solicitation and directed them to the website to download the RFP and supporting documentation. On April 14, 2021, sealed bids were accepted and opened virtually, and two proposals were received.

The initial tabulated results were: TEL Systems, base bid $42,948.00; and MOSS Audio, base bid $45,183.96. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution, and acceptance of the RFP terms and conditions.

During evaluation, it was noted that both bidders provided PLM bonds, which are not required for proposals less than $50,000.00; those bond amounts were subtracted from both bidders' base bids. Additionally, TEL Systems' bid did not meet the technical requirements stated in the RFP and during the pre-bid meeting, so using their installed unit pricing the evaluator revised their bid to reconcile both bids to the technical requirements. The reconciled figures were presented as follows: MOSS Audio, base bid $45,183.96, less a PLM bond of $312.81, with $0 technical reconciliation, for a total of $44,871.15; and TEL Systems, base bid $42,948.00, less a PLM bond of $295.00, less a technical reconciliation of $3,224.00, for a total of $45,877.00.

Based on this analysis, Convergent recommends the award of the THS Media Center AV (RFP #9926) project to the reconciled low bid from MOSS Audio in the amount of $44,871.15, with an additional approximately 5% contingency of $2,250.00, for a total of $47,121.15. The letter invites questions at 810-223-0531 and is signed by Eric Helsel, RCDD/OSP/RTPM, Project Manager, Convergent Technology Partners. This total of $47,121.15 matches the amount in the companion Board resolution (agenda item 8.C) awarding the bid to Moss Audio.

The Enterprise Wide Executive Summary and Budget Assumptions for the Oakland Schools Fiscal Year 2021-22 original proposed budget, dated March 2021 (document references 3.16.21). Oakland Schools is the Intermediate School District (ISD) serving Oakland County, including Troy School District, and this document was included in the May 18, 2021 Troy Board of Education packet for information.

Agency overview: Oakland Schools is described as one of 56 Intermediate School Districts established in Michigan in 1962. ISDs are regional service agencies providing support services to constituent districts that are best delivered regionally by cost, size, and quality. Oakland Schools is an autonomous, tax-supported public school district governed by Michigan General School Law. Its stated mission is "Oakland Schools: Learning today. Transforming tomorrow." The document lists organizational beliefs and direction emphasizing service, student achievement, collaboration, ethical behavior, and partnership with the Oakland County community, government, business, and social agencies.

How it is funded: Proposed total funding for fiscal year 2021-22 is $359.6 million, comprising property taxes of $207.6 million; other local revenue and investment revenue of $32.2 million; state source revenue of $18.8 million; other financing sources and indirect revenue of $8.9 million; expected new grant award funding of $78.6 million; and estimated grant carryover funding of $13.5 million. Funding is presented net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund revenues.

How resources are used: Proposed total expenditures for fiscal year 2021-22 are $364.3 million, comprising salary, wage and benefits of $76.4 million; purchased services, supplies, and dues/fees of $20.3 million; electric and natural gas utilities of $0.9 million; capital outlay of $5.6 million; transfers to LEAs and other funds of $166.0 million; grant related expenditures of $92.1 million; and payment on existing debt of $3.0 million. Expenditures are presented net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund expenses.

What's new or of special significance: On the revenue side, property tax revenue is budgeted to increase by 2.7%, or $5.5 million. Tax revenues have increased a total of 23% since the end of the recession in 2014; however, as of FY 2020-21 they remain $14.8 million below pre-recession levels. While taxable values in Oakland County are expected to increase more than 3.75%, the district anticipates another Headlee rollback for FY 2021-22 due to the low rate of inflation, which if imposed would mark the seventh consecutive year of Headlee rollbacks. Tax abatements have leveled off after peaking in fiscal years 2012 and 2013, though the full economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic remains undetermined and the environment is described as ripe for an increase in tax tribunal challenges; the district holds reserves for anticipated abatement losses. It lays out five guiding principles, traces the district's history from the 2009 TSD Diversity Study forward, and describes a three-priority framework of Assess, Connect, and Engage. The presentation highlights results from an Equity and Inclusion Survey conducted by Hanover Research reflecting 7,448 stakeholder perceptions, whose key finding was that the greatest opportunity for improvement lies in the experiences of Black students and Black parents.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A PowerPoint workshop presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education (May 18, 2021 meeting) outlining the district's Equity and Inclusion program, led by Cornelius Godfrey, Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships.

Guiding Principles (5)
Radical Equity, Gracious Inclusion, Abundance Mentality, Fearless Feedback, and Many Hands.

History ("Where we've been")
- 2009 TSD Diversity Study by R&J Consulting Group (Rosalind Cox), with findings/recommendations on personnel diversity, cultural awareness, curriculum, and parent outreach
- Diversity Council meetings convened 2011-2012
- Current work: National Equity Project, Teacher's College TRWP, book clubs, an Excellence in Equity Statement, "Leading for Equity," training from Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools, and an equity survey by Hanover Research

Three Priorities framework
- Assess: baseline current equity, center marginalized perspectives, gauge efficacy
- Connect: build stakeholder coalitions, community and student advisory boards, feedback channels
- Engage: draft vision/mission, accountability platform, 3-5 year strategic plan, professional development

Survey findings
Equity & Inclusion Survey reflected 7,448 stakeholder perceptions: 5,520 students (grades 5-12), 1,503 parents, and 425 TSD staff. Key finding: the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. Final report expected late May/early June 2021.

Purpose
To brief the Board on the equity vision, its historical context, the operating framework, and preliminary survey results.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is a slide presentation delivered as a Board workshop on the Troy School District's Equity and Inclusion (E&I) initiative at the May 18, 2021 regular Board of Education meeting. The named presenter/author is Cornelius Godfrey, who holds the newly created role of Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships.

Guiding Principles: The presentation articulates five guiding principles: (1) Radical Equity — dismantling systems of inequity requires courage, imagination, and a high tolerance for discomfort; (2) Gracious Inclusion — extending invitations to "the table" not on the basis of perceived merit; (3) Abundance Mentality — believing available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child; (4) Fearless Feedback — actively seeking critique without threat of reprisal; and (5) Many Hands — framing the work as "our work."

Where we've been: The district's equity history includes the 2009 TSD Diversity Study conducted by R&J Consulting Group (Rosalind Cox) and a Diversity Council that convened meetings between 2011 and 2012. Study findings and recommendations addressed personnel diversity (reviewing hiring/recruiting with a focus on retention), cultural awareness (appointing a diversity council, establishing staff-wide competencies, incorporating them into evaluation), curriculum (reviewing achievement/access gaps and materials for inclusivity), and parent outreach (establishing parent networks).

Where we are: Current efforts involve the National Equity Project (district and building administrators, teachers, students); Teacher's College TRWP (teachers); book clubs (elementary/secondary teachers, administrators, support staff); an Excellence in Equity Statement (Board of Education); "Leading for Equity" (teachers and support staff as early adopters); building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching led by Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools; and an Equity Survey by Hanover Research covering all stakeholders.

Where we're going: The plan calls for system-wide integration across all pillars, departments, and content areas; significant investment from Teaching & Learning; community voice through collaborative meetings; quantitative evidence; the creation of the new equity role; and an equity agenda implementing a comprehensive framework of supports at building and district levels (BELE), a learning continuum for all TSD employees, capacity-building through stakeholder partnerships, transparency and reporting mechanisms, and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

Three Priorities: The framework organizes work into (1) Assess — establish a baseline for current equity, inclusion, and community relations; center marginalized perspectives; gauge efficacy and implementation fidelity, using a comprehensive "Listening Tour" of surveys, interviews, questionnaires, focus groups, plus a quantitative data deep dive into disparities in perceptions, discipline, and academic outcomes, a community connections review, and curriculum review; (2) Connect — assemble Community and Student Advisory Boards, develop a district-wide staff coalition, establish feedback channels, and partner with equity exemplars; and (3) Engage — draft vision and mission statements, implement an accountability/transparency platform, develop a 3-5 year strategic plan, develop research-based criteria, provide professional development, and establish norms for dialogue. A "pulley analogy" is used to illustrate how connections multiply the effort of engagement.

Survey results: The Equity and Inclusion Survey (by Hanover Research) reflected 7,448 stakeholder perceptions, comprising 5,520 students (grades 5-12), 1,503 parents, and 425 TSD staff members. The key finding stated that the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents, with the final report expected in late May or early June 2021. Later slides compared overall stakeholder perceptions against those of Black stakeholders and parents (chart content truncated).

What it is
A budget transmittal letter dated April 5, 2021, from Oakland Schools to the Troy School District Board of Education (a "Board of Education Designate"), submitting Oakland Schools' proposed FY 2021-22 budget for statutory review. Under Michigan School Code Section 380.624(2), the proposed General Fund budget must be submitted to constituent districts, and only the General Fund budget is voted on by those districts.

Key figures / features
- Projected growth in Oakland Schools property tax revenue: 2.7%; a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is considered probable for FY 2021-22
- COVID-19 response in 2020-21 (subsidies for Illuminate DnA, Oakland HR Consortium, elimination of ONE Network fees, reduced Shared Services IGA fees, CTE funding actions, 100% CTE transportation costs) saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million
- Estimated $2 million in 2021-22 for additional student learning and teacher professional learning (Oakland Youth Innovation Lab, Design Studio, tutoring, OSTC supplemental instruction)
- Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO): five-year, $5 million early-literacy project launched 2019-20
- CTE: added funds for program redesign and a CTE mobile classroom ("STEMi"); CTE allocation to LEAs increased more than 25% in 2019-20 and maintained

Who/what
Oakland Schools serves Oakland County constituent districts. Technology services are provided to fifteen districts; business office services to four via intergovernmental agreements (IGAs). References the MiPEER Consortium formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 districts.

Purpose
To satisfy the statutory review requirement and inform Troy's Board about the ISD budget before the Designates meeting and board resolution.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is a budget transmittal letter dated April 5, 2021, addressed to a "Board of Education Designate," through which the Oakland Schools Board of Education invites the Troy School District Board of Education to review Oakland Schools' proposed FY 2021-22 budget. It was included in the Troy Board's May 18, 2021 meeting packet. The letter explains that, per Michigan School Code Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2021-22 General Fund budget must be submitted to each constituent district's Board of Education for review; while Oakland Schools includes budgets for all its funds for transparency, only the General Fund budget is voted upon by constituent districts. Details on the timing of the Designates meeting and the required board resolution appear near the letter's end.

Revenue outlook: Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars and projects a 2.7% growth factor in property tax revenues. These projections are described as conservative relative to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is considered probable for FY 2021-22 — this occurs when annual growth on existing property exceeds the rate of inflation (CPI). Additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor was expected by June 1.

COVID-19 response: The response began in 2020-21 with subsidies for Illuminate DnA and the Oakland Human Resource Consortium, elimination of ONE Network fees, reduction in Shared Services IGA fees, carryover of CTE Regional Allocation funding, and payment of 100% of CTE transportation costs — actions that saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million in 2020-21. Oakland Schools reduced budgets in 2020-21 for travel, conference fees, printing, and certain purchased services, then reinstated those budgets for 2021-22 as operations return toward pre-pandemic status. Support resources include guidance for evaluating well-being in school communities, best practices for remote/hybrid teaching, and curriculum/instruction/assessment toolkits. For 2021-22, Oakland Schools is providing an estimated $2 million for additional learning opportunities for students and professional learning for teachers, including the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab, Design Studio, tutoring, and OSTC Supplemental Instruction. Additional financial support to local districts in 2021-22 includes a full subsidy of Illuminate DnA base costs and allowing districts to carry over the unspent portion of their CTE Regional Allocation from 2020-21. The letter notes Oakland Schools, unlike local districts, has not received ESSER Fund, Governor's Emergency Education Relief Fund, or Coronavirus Relief Fund monies and will not receive ESSER II funding; its COVID-19 expenditures are funded with tax revenues and state aid ISD funding.

Program initiatives: The Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO) Project, focused on early literacy success for children in Oakland County, is a five-year, $5 million project launched during the 2019-20 school year, developed to be research-based, capacity-building, tailored to district needs, and focused on job-embedded professional learning. For Career and Technical Education (CTE), aligned with the Michigan Department of Education's "Top 10 in 10 Years" goals, Oakland Schools dedicates additional resources to its four technical campuses and includes funds for career program redesign and initial funding for a CTE mobile classroom (the "STEMi") to bring STEM activities to local districts beginning Spring 2020-21; the CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25% in 2019-20 and maintained in 2021-22. Shared Services provided to Oakland County districts on a cost-recovery basis include technology, business office, instruction, and truancy services; technology services are provided to fifteen constituent districts and business office services to four districts through intergovernmental agreements (IGAs). The letter also references the MiPEER Consortium (Michigan Partnership for Essential..., text truncated), formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts.

The 2020-21 Budget Amendment Resolution, agenda item 6.D. on the CONSENT agenda of the June 15, 2021 regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education. The resolution amends and approves the general appropriations and budget of the Troy School District for fiscal year 2020-21 and is to be made part of the official minutes; the cover notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be entered into the minutes. It bundles several fund amendments: General Fund Amendment 2, Food Service Fund Amendment 2, Troy Career Center Fund Amendment 1, Community Service Fund Amendment 2, Troy School District Preschool Fund Amendment 2, Facilities Rental Fund Amendment 2, Troy School and Student Activities Fund Amendment 1, Early Childhood Learning Capital Projects Fund Amendment 1, and Sinking Fund Amendment 2.

The amended appropriations by fund are: General Fund $165,691,478; Food Service Fund $2,437,400; Troy Career Center Fund $2,508,370; Community Service Fund $654,229; Troy School District Preschool Fund $1,338,805; Facilities Rental Fund $106,501; Troy School and Student Activities Fund $700,000; Early Childhood Learning Center Capital Projects Fund $370,884; and Sinking Fund Capital Projects Fund $1,500,000.

For the General Fund, the resolution amends estimated revenues and unappropriated fund balance. Revenues move from the prior amended budget to the newly amended budget as follows: Local $41,190,814 to $40,829,084 (a decrease of $361,730); State $106,107,940 to $109,882,333 (an increase of $3,774,393); Federal $10,345,058 to $10,657,319 (an increase of $312,261); and Incoming Transfers & Other $10,297,749 to $10,188,368 (a decrease of $109,381). Total Revenues, Incoming Transfers & Other rise from $167,941,561 to $171,557,104, an increase of $3,615,543. Fund Balance at July 1 is $26,009,710 (unchanged), making the total available to appropriate $197,566,814 (up from $193,951,271), of which $165,691,478 is appropriated.

General Fund expenditures are set out by function. Instruction: Basic Programs $86,444,895 to $87,613,549 (+$1,168,654); Added Needs $22,186,662 to $21,550,665 (-$635,997); Adult & Continuing Education $1,066,404 to $792,672 (-$273,732); Total Instruction $109,697,961 to $109,956,886 (+$258,925). Support Services: Pupil $11,947,566 to $12,003,769 (+$56,203); Instructional Staff $11,189,807 to $11,103,220 (-$86,587); General Administration $1,206,375 to $1,162,049 (-$44,326); School Administration $8,826,046 to $9,030,733 (+$204,687); Business Services $1,726,938 to $1,669,622 (-$57,316); Operations & Maintenance $11,123,109 to $11,742,577 (+$619,468); Pupil Transportation $3,461,929 to $2,883,297 (-$578,632); Central Services $3,248,574 to $2,901,250 (-$347,324); Athletics $1,753,670 to $1,624,427 (-$129,243); Total Support Services $54,484,014 to $54,120,944 (-$363,070).

The Food Service Fund is likewise amended: revenues Local $35,000 to $30,000 (-$5,000), State $133,234 to $110,416 (-$22,818), and Federal $2,245,155 to $2,325,155 (+$80,000), for total revenues of $2,413,389 to $2,465,571 (+$52,182); with a July 1 fund balance of $90,645, total available to appropriate of $2,556,216, and $2,437,400 appropriated (Food Services expenditures rising from $2,293,936 to $2,437,400, +$143,464). The document is structured as a suggested resolution with lines for a mover, a supporter, and Yes/No votes, adopted as part of the official minutes of the June 15, 2021 regular meeting.
